title: Onboarding that respects a busy user's time
metaTitle: User onboarding UX that respects time
excerpt: User onboarding UX should start with the person's job and show a result before the tour. Accounts and tutorials can wait until that result is real.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band. They are looking at the work on the screen, which is the moment onboarding should reach quickly.
caption: Show the job before the tour. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should we ask for an account before the person sees the product?
faqs.answer: Ask only for what the first result requires. If they can see a useful result before you store anything, let them. When the job truly needs an account, a payment method, or permission, ask at that moment and say why. A signup wall in front of an empty tour spends the only attention you might get.

faqs.question: Where do tooltips and product tours belong?
faqs.answer: After the person has done the thing once, and only on the step they are likely to miss next. A tour that explains the whole product up front assumes they will remember it. They will not. A sentence on the empty screen, and a confirmation when the action works, teaches more than a sequence of spotlights.

faqs.question: How do we onboard someone who was invited by a teammate?
faqs.answer: Put them inside the work they were invited to do, with the inviter's context visible. Skip the company-wide slideshow. Their job is the shared object, not a settings checklist. Offer the checklist later, from a place they can ignore until they need it.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
User onboarding UX that respects time starts with the person's job and shows a result before it explains the product. Accounts, profile fields, and tutorials wait until that result exists, unless the result is impossible without them. A first session spent on orientation is a session spent not doing the thing they came to do.

People arrive with a task and a limited willingness to prepare. The product can honor that by letting the task happen, or it can spend the visit on a tour of navigation. The tour feels responsible in a planning meeting. In the first session it is a delay. Design the delay out, and keep only the questions you need in order to show something true.

## Start from the job they already have

Write the first session as the smallest version of the real job. A scheduler sends one real invite. A bookkeeper sees one real unpaid invoice, or creates one. A teammate joining a workspace lands on the document they were invited to, not on a carnival of empty charts about the whole company.

If you do not know the job yet, you are not ready to design the opening. Guessing a generic "welcome" flow produces generic steps: name, role, company size, theme, tour. Those steps are about you learning marketing attributes. They are not about them finishing anything. Collect attributes later, if you still want them, after the person has a reason to stay.

Say the job in the first sentence on the screen. Not the category you hope to rank for. The task. "Send today's schedule to the crew." Then put the control for that task in reach. Secondary setup can live behind a quiet link for people who truly need it first. The default path is the work.

## Show a result, then explain

The moment of value is a real object in the product: a sent message, a saved record, a comparison they needed. Reach it in as few steps as you can without lying. Sample data is a last resort, and only when it is marked as a sample and can be cleared. A fictional success teaches the interface and leaves the person with cleanup. A real success teaches the interface and leaves them with their work.

Nielsen Norman Group reported in 2011 that people often leave a web page within 10 to 20 seconds, and that earning a longer visit depends on making the value clear within about 10 seconds. They also found that visitors read only about a quarter of the text on pages they actually open. [The article](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) measured web pages, not every app, and the caution still applies to a first run. A five-slide tour spends the window in which they decide to stay. Put the value in the first view. Let explanation follow the action, in one sentence, at the moment it becomes relevant.

Confirmation is part of the result. Say what happened and what is next, in the same nouns as the button they pressed. Then stop. A modal that celebrates and then starts a second tour has taken the result away. Let them look at the thing they just made.

## Defer the account, the fields, and the tour

Ask for an account when you need to store something on their behalf, or when the product is meaningless without identity. Ask for a payment method when they are about to pay. Ask for a role or a company size when it changes the product in a way they can see. Each question should be easy to justify in one line on the screen. "We use this to send the schedule" is a justification. "Help us personalize your experience" is a stall.

Required fields are a cost. Every extra field is a chance they leave before the result. If a field is for your analytics, it is not required, and it may not belong in the first session at all. You can ask tomorrow, inside the product, from a person who has already succeeded once.

Tours and tooltip chains belong after the first success, and only on a step people actually miss. If nobody misses it, you do not need the spotlight. A permanent coach mark on a button the person can already read is nagging. One hint, dismissible, tied to a real next action, is enough. Write it as a sentence, not as a character who talks.

There is a case for a short setup when the product cannot show anything true without it. Connecting a calendar, inviting the other person who must approve, or choosing the single workspace they were hired into. Keep that setup inside the job. Show the consequence of each answer immediately. A wizard that collects five facts and then dumps the person on a blank home has hidden the result at the end of a form. Reorder it so the first fact produces a visible change.

## Invited people are a different first session

Someone who arrives from an invite already has context. They should see the object they were invited to, the name of the person who invited them, and the action they are expected to take. A second onboarding that re-explains the company is a tax on the inviter's credibility.

Skip the slideshow. Offer deeper setup, such as notification choices, from a place they can find later. Default the notifications to something sane and visible, so silence is a choice they can reverse. The worst first hour is a person who cannot find the document, followed by a week of email they did not mean to turn on.

Administrators setting up a workspace for other people have yet another job. Their onboarding is the setup, and it should be labeled as setup. Do not force every later user through the administrator's checklist. Two paths, clearly separated, respect both clocks.

## What to measure without building a research program

Watch where the first session stops. If people quit on a field, the field is a candidate to move or delete. If they quit during a tour, the tour is in the way. If they reach the result and do not return, the result may not have been valuable, which is a product problem rather than a copy problem. You do not need a large sample to notice a stop that happens to almost everyone you ask.

Hanabi designs the first session as part of the interface, with the empty state and the success written before the tour is even considered. The empty screen often does the teaching a carousel was going to do, in fewer words. That is a better use of the person's time, and it is a smaller thing to maintain when the product changes.

The screens that carry this are the blank, the success, and the failure. If those are still generic, fix them before you add a walkthrough. The next piece explains them: [empty states, errors, and the screens teams forget](/blog/empty-states-and-errors).
